newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Asian culture crucial to insurance growth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asian culture crucial to insurance growth.

text.p: Recognising cultural differences will be the crucial factor in life insurance marketing in Asia, industry analysts say, adding that Western insurers targeting the potentially lucrative market will fail if they ignore it.

"Asia is not how the U.S. or Europe were 30 years ago. It has technology, culture and infrastructure and the market must be approached from this perspective," said Andrew Giffin, principal with consulting actuaries Tillinghast-Towers Perrin in the United States.
He said Western players could not take it for granted that successful products at home would also go over big in Asia.
"Insurers must offer products uniquely designed to fit Asian needs," Giffin said.

And the Asian influence would be exerted even more strongly as the balance of economic power shifted to East from West, said Alan Gemes, managing partner with the Hong Kong office of management consultant Coopers & Lybrand.
"There is a major shift in consumer behaviour in buying financial services and we are in the midst of this," he said.
SOPHISTICATION GROWING IN ASIA
Life insurance is increasingly bought by -- instead of sold to -- Asian consumers, indicating growing sophistication and product knowledge, Gemes said.
As Asia becomes the focus of the global insurance market, huge changes will come in marketing, what policies covered as standard and how companies operated in the market, he said.
Giffen and Gemes were speaking at the two-day Pan-Asia Insurance Summit in Hong Kong in February, a gathering of senior insurance industry executives from three continents.
Asia already accounts for about half of global life insurance premiums and that number will rise as the region becomes more affluent, analysts say.
Industry executives predict premiums in Asia will grow by 10 percent annually for the next decade, while the West can expect a more sedate growth rate of four percent a year.

But while life is the most important class of business in emerging insurance markets, both eastern and western companies face problems in marketing products that pay only on death, a subject on which Asian culture is particularly sensitive.

"There is a psychological barrier still inherent in the culture because when an Indonesian thinks about life insurance, he thinks about death," said Billy Sindoro, president of Lippo Life Insurance Company in Jakarta.
TAKAFUL PRODUCTS SET TO SHAPE GLOBAL MARKET
The potential of Asia to shape the global insurance market has been seen most strongly in the development of Takaful insurance, designed with Moslem religious sensitivities in mind.
Takaful, which means helping one another, is growing in popularity in Asia and could come to dominate the portfolios of every insurer all over the world, according to one industry leader.
"Will Takaful become the dominant form of insurance? Let me put it this way -- Moslems make up half the population of the world," said the president of the Life Insurance Association of Malaysia.
Ezamshah Ismail said Takaful products were cost transparent on religious grounds and had built-in safeguards on commission disclosure, an area that the West is creating new regulations to handle.

Pensions scandals in Britain and the United States, sparked by allegations of agents selling policies to maximise commissions and failing in their duty to give the best advice to consumers, were unlikely to be seen in Takaful-based markets, said Ismail.
"Takaful is very transparent. It has changed people's perspectives and its impact is that not only Moslems but non-Moslems are buying the products," he said.
Bahrain-based Arab Insurance Group has estimated the Islamic insurance market will be worth $2.1 billion worldwide by the year 2010.
